claim: Children who survive severe malaria are frequently reinfected and experience episodes of febrile malaria with similar or even higher parasite densities.
source: Crucially, this study further showed that children who survive severe malaria are frequently reinfected and experience episodes of febrile malaria with similar or even higher parasite densities (Gonçalves et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published study (Gonçalves et al., 2014) that documented reinfection patterns in children.

claim: Immunity to severe forms of malaria is not due to improved parasite elimination (resistance) but instead underpinned by the improved ability of the host to limit the pathological consequences of infection (tolerance).
source: Immunity to severe forms of malaria is therefore not due to improved parasite elimination (resistance) but instead underpinned by the improved ability of the host to limit the pathological consequences of infection (tolerance).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that children are reinfected with similar or higher parasite densities yet do not develop severe disease.

claim: Acute malaria infection causes hypoglycaemia and the ability to maintain blood glucose levels can determine life or death.
source: for example, acute infection causes hypoglycaemia and so the ability to maintain blood glucose levels within dynamic range – in crosstalk with iron metabolism (Weis et al., 2017) – can determine life or death (Cumnock et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies (Weis et al., 2017; Cumnock et al., 2018) that demonstrate the role of glucose homeostasis in malaria survival.

claim: The induction of heme oxygenase-1 by nitric oxide leads to the detoxification of free heme, which protects renal proximal tubule epithelial cells and prevents acute kidney injury.
source: Furthermore, the induction of heme oxygenase-1 by nitric oxide (Jeney et al., 2014) leads to the detoxification of free heme, which is released from ruptured red cells (Seixas et al., 2009) – this protects renal proximal tubule epithelial cells and prevents acute kidney injury (Ramos et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies (Jeney et al., 2014; Seixas et al., 2009; Ramos et al., 2019) that demonstrate the protective role of heme oxygenase-1.

claim: Lower levels of circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines are found in children in Malawi who survive severe malaria compared to those who succumb.
source: Field data support the idea that dampening the inflammatory response to P. falciparum affords protection; lower levels of circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines are found in children in Malawi who survive severe malaria compared to those who succumb (Mandala et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published study (Mandala et al., 2017) that measured cytokine levels in children with severe malaria.

claim: Ghanaian children in a high transmission area have higher parasite densities but less systemic inflammation and fewer febrile episodes than children in a lower transmission setting.
source: And critically, inflammation can be reduced in the absence of improved parasite control; Ghanaian children in a high transmission area have higher parasite densities but less systemic inflammation and fewer febrile episodes than children in a lower transmission setting (Ademolue et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published study (Ademolue et al., 2017) that compared children in different transmission settings.

claim: Human monocytes produce less pro-inflammatory cytokines when stimulated after an episode of febrile malaria as compared to before.
source: Innate memory has been shown to operate independently of pathogen load (Dominguez-Andres and Netea, 2019; Seeley and Ghosh, 2017) and human monocytes produce less pro-inflammatory cytokines when stimulated after an episode of febrile malaria as compared to before (Portugal et al., 2014), suggesting that they are intrinsically modified by infection.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies (Dominguez-Andres and Netea, 2019; Seeley and Ghosh, 2017; Portugal et al., 2014) that demonstrate innate memory in monocytes.

claim: P. chabaudi AS causes a mild infection, characterised by a low pathogen load and few clinical symptoms.
source: P. chabaudi AS causes a mild infection, characterised by a low pathogen load and few clinical symptoms (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A-C which displays parasitemia and red cell counts for AS infection.

claim: P. chabaudi AJ leads to acute hyperparasitaemia and severe anaemia, accompanied by hypothermia and prostration.
source: In contrast, P. chabaudi AJ (which has more than 140,000 SNPs cf. P. chabaudi AS [Otto et al., 2014]) leads to acute hyperparasitaemia and severe anaemia (Figure 1B–C), accompanied by hypothermia and prostration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Otto et al., 2014 for SNP information.

claim: P. chabaudi AJ has more than 140,000 SNPs compared to P. chabaudi AS.
source: In contrast, P. chabaudi AJ (which has more than 140,000 SNPs cf. P. chabaudi AS [Otto et al., 2014]) leads to acute hyperparasitaemia and severe anaemia (Figure 1B–C), accompanied by hypothermia and prostration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Otto et al., 2014 which characterized genetic differences between parasite strains.

claim: P. chabaudi AS sequesters in key immune sites such as bone marrow and spleen.
source: AJ shares many key features with AS such as synchrony, chronicity and a persisting low-grade anaemia (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), and yet whilst AS sequesters in key immune sites such as bone marrow and spleen (Brugat et al., 2014) we find no evidence that AJ sequesters in host tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brugat et al., 2014 and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: P. chabaudi AJ does not sequester in host tissues.
source: AJ shares many key features with AS such as synchrony, chronicity and a persisting low-grade anaemia (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), and yet whilst AS sequesters in key immune sites such as bone marrow and spleen (Brugat et al., 2014) we find no evidence that AJ sequesters in host tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D which shows sequestration rates in various organs.

claim: The bone marrow quickly prioritises myelopoiesis by increasing the number of granulocyte monocyte progenitors (GMP) during acute malaria infection.
source: We found that the bone marrow quickly prioritises myelopoiesis by increasing the number of granulocyte monocyte progenitors (GMP) (Figure 1D, see Supplementary file 1 for gating strategies).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D which displays GMP counts during infection.

claim: An increased number of inflammatory monocytes and neutrophils are released into circulation and recruited into the spleen during acute malaria infection.
source: Consequently, an increased number of inflammatory monocytes and neutrophils are released into circulation and recruited into their target organ – the spleen (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A which display monocyte and neutrophil counts.

claim: Megakaryocyte erythroid progenitors (MEP) appear de novo in the spleen during acute malaria infection.
source: Furthermore, megakaryocyte erythroid progenitors (MEP) appear de novo in the spleen (Figure 1E); this extramedullary mechanism of erythropoiesis likely represents a division of labour in an attempt to compensate for the loss of erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow (Pathak and Ghosh, 2016).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Pathak and Ghosh, 2016 regarding extramedullary erythropoiesis.

claim: Long-lived prenatally seeded tissue-resident macrophages in bone marrow and spleen rapidly disappear during acute malaria infection.
source: Remarkably, we found that long-lived prenatally seeded tissue-resident macrophages in bone marrow and spleen (Hashimoto et al., 2013) rapidly disappear during acute infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1G and citation to Hashimoto et al., 2013 regarding tissue-resident macrophages.

claim: Red pulp macrophages are the only cells that can store and recycle iron in the spleen.
source: Since red pulp macrophages are the only cells that can store and recycle iron in the spleen their disappearance thus means that ferric iron, which can be revealed histologically with Prussian Blue staining, is completely absent at the peak of infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about red pulp macrophage function, supported by histological data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Ferric iron is completely absent in the spleen at the peak of acute malaria infection.
source: Since red pulp macrophages are the only cells that can store and recycle iron in the spleen their disappearance thus means that ferric iron, which can be revealed histologically with Prussian Blue staining, is completely absent at the peak of infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E using Prussian Blue staining.

claim: Patrolling monocytes disappear early in malaria infection.
source: We could further demonstrate that patrolling monocytes (Carlin et al., 2013), often regarded as the tissue-resident macrophages of the vasculature (Mildner et al., 2017), also disappear early in infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1G and citations to Carlin et al., 2013 and Mildner et al., 2017 regarding patrolling monocyte identity.

claim: More than one third of all gene ontology terms in spleen monocytes during acute infection were related to host defence.
source: When we merged all linked nodes into supergroups (see Materials and methods) we found that more than one third of all GO terms were related to host defence (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by clueGO analysis data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: ClueGO identified interferon signaling as an upstream regulator of monocyte fate during acute malaria infection.
source: Furthermore, clueGO identified interferon signaling as an upstream regulator of monocyte fate (Figure 2B); in agreement, interferon-inducible guanylate binding proteins were highly upregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by clueGO analysis shown in Figure 2B and gene expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Interferon-inducible guanylate binding proteins were highly upregulated in spleen monocytes during acute malaria infection.
source: Furthermore, clueGO identified interferon signaling as an upstream regulator of monocyte fate (Figure 2B); in agreement, interferon-inducible guanylate binding proteins were highly upregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Monocytes initiate a transcriptional programme typical of terminally differentiated inflammatory macrophages during acute malaria infection.
source: This revealed that monocytes initiate a transcriptional programme that is typical of terminally differentiated inflammatory macrophages (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data of signature genes shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Monocytes upregulate expression of hallmark cytokines and chemokines associated with a type I inflammatory response during acute malaria infection.
source: They upregulate their ability to sense parasite- and host-derived danger signals by increasing transcription of diverse pattern recognition receptors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and upregulate expression of the hallmark cytokines and chemokines associated with a type I inflammatory response (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Monocytes enhance their capacity to engage T cell immunity by upregulating all major components of the antigen processing and presentation machinery during acute malaria infection.
source: Furthermore, they enhance their capacity to engage T cell immunity by upregulating all major components of the antigen processing and presentation machinery (for class I and class II MHC), and attempt to fine-tune T cell activation by increasing their expression of co-stimulatory molecules and checkpoint inhibitors (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: A clear Warburg effect was not observed in vivo in monocytes in response to malaria.
source: Notably, a clear Warburg effect – the metabolic switch from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis described when monocytes are stimulated with LPS in vitro (Cheng et al., 2014) – was not observed in vivo in response to malaria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation enzymes were induced, contrasting with the expected Warburg effect described by Cheng et al., 2014.

claim: The key enzymes involved in both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation were transcriptionally induced in monocytes during acute malaria infection.
source: Instead, the key enzymes involved in both metabolic pathways were transcriptionally induced (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The response of myeloid and progenitor cells in bone marrow, blood, and spleen was remarkably similar between P. chabaudi AS and AJ infections.
source: Surprisingly, despite substantial differences in parasite density and patterns of sequestration (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) the response of myeloid and progenitor cells in bone marrow, blood, and spleen was remarkably similar between AS and AJ (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C comparing AS and AJ infections.

claim: The fate and function of spleen monocytes was essentially identical between P. chabaudi AS and AJ infections.
source: Moreover, the fate and function of spleen monocytes was essentially identical – a direct pairwise comparison identified only a single differentially expressed gene (Kelch34) between the two models.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing analysis that identified only one differentially expressed gene between AS and AJ.

claim: A direct pairwise comparison identified only a single differentially expressed gene (Kelch34) between monocytes from AS and AJ infected mice.
source: Moreover, the fate and function of spleen monocytes was essentially identical – a direct pairwise comparison identified only a single differentially expressed gene (Kelch34) between the two models.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing analysis comparing AS and AJ infections.

claim: The four largest supergroups in monocytes isolated from AJ-infected mice also dominated the response to AS infection.
source: In turn, clueGO analysis revealed that the four largest supergroups in monocytes isolated from AJ-infected mice (Figure 2B–C) also dominated the response to AS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by clueGO analysis data shown in Figure 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Parasite genotype, pathogen load, and the sequestration of infected red cells in immune tissues does not fundamentally alter the myeloid response to acute malaria infection.
source: It therefore appears that parasite genotype, pathogen load, and the sequestration of infected red cells in immune tissues does not fundamentally alter the myeloid response to acute infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that AS and AJ infections produce similar myeloid responses despite differences in these parameters.

claim: The spleen stops extramedullary erythropoiesis during chronic malaria infection.
source: Despite this abundance of parasite-derived signals, the spleen stops extramedullary erythropoiesis and creates new structural demarkations between red and white pulp (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and histology data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The spleen creates new structural demarkations between red and white pulp during chronic malaria infection.
source: Despite this abundance of parasite-derived signals, the spleen stops extramedullary erythropoiesis and creates new structural demarkations between red and white pulp (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by histology data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The bone marrow reduces the production of granulocyte monocyte progenitors during chronic malaria infection.
source: Furthermore, the bone marrow reduces the production of granulocyte monocyte progenitors, which in turn reduces the number of inflammatory monocytes and neutrophils trafficking into the blood and spleen (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Resident macrophages begin to repopulate their tissue niches during chronic malaria infection.
source: At the same time, resident macrophages begin to repopulate their tissue niches (Figure 1G) and ferric iron stores are re-established in the spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1G and histology data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Ferric iron stores are re-established in the spleen during chronic malaria infection.
source: At the same time, resident macrophages begin to repopulate their tissue niches (Figure 1G) and ferric iron stores are re-established in the spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by Prussian Blue staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Naive hosts quickly adapt to tolerate malaria parasites and return the myeloid compartment towards a healthy uninfected baseline.
source: These data provide compelling evidence that naive hosts quickly adapt to tolerate malaria parasites and return the myeloid compartment towards a healthy uninfected baseline.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations that during chronic infection, emergency myelopoiesis is reduced, tissue architecture is restored, and macrophages repopulate.

claim: The transcriptome of monocytes during chronic infection is almost indistinguishable from uninfected controls.
source: In agreement, the transcriptome of monocytes during chronic infection is almost indistinguishable from uninfected controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A comparing chronic infection to uninfected controls.

claim: Monocytes are no longer programmed to differentiate into inflammatory macrophages during chronic malaria infection.
source: Monocytes are no longer programmed to differentiate into inflammatory macrophages upon their arrival in the spleen (Figure 2D) and they silence transcriptional signatures of the acute phase response (Figure 2E–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2D, 2E-G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: There is no evidence that monocytes engage mechanisms to suppress inflammation during chronic malaria infection.
source: Notably, we find no evidence that they engage mechanisms to suppress inflammation, such as regulatory cytokines (IL-10 and TGFβ) or inhibitors of T cell activation (PD-L1) (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2E and G showing no upregulation of these genes.

claim: Monocytes adopt a state of quiescence during chronic malaria infection despite persisting parasitaemia.
source: Instead, monocytes simply adopt a state of quiescence during chronic infection despite persisting parasitaemia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that monocytes have minimal transcriptional changes compared to uninfected controls despite ongoing parasitemia.

claim: Quiescence of monocytes during chronic infection is reversible.
source: Importantly, we can show that quiescence is reversible – when monocytes are removed from the spleen of chronically infected mice and stimulated in vitro with LPS their inflammatory response is comparable to monocytes from uninfected mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro LPS stimulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Monocytes from chronically infected mice stimulated with LPS in vitro show the Warburg effect and transcription of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and co-stimulatory molecules.
source: In both cases, we clearly observe the Warburg effect and transcription of a plethora of inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and co-stimulatory molecules, together with the induction of Nos2 – the best biomarker of an inflammatory macrophage fate (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from LPS-stimulated monocytes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-D.

claim: Monocytes are not in a permanent refractory state during chronic malaria infection.
source: Clearly, monocytes are not in a permanent refractory state during chronic infection; instead, their activation and differentiation in response to parasites and their pyrogenic products must somehow be silenced in the remodelled spleen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that monocytes can respond to LPS stimulation in vitro, indicating they are not permanently refractory.

claim: Parasite burden is matched between first and second infection in the reinfection model.
source: In this model, parasite burden (Figure 3B) and the dynamics of red cell loss (Figure 3C) are both matched between first and second infection – this eliminates pathogen load as a confounding factor when analysing acquired mechanisms of disease tolerance.
evidence: Supported by parasitemia data shown in Figure 3B comparing first and second infections.

claim: The dynamics of red cell loss are matched between first and second infection in the reinfection model.
source: In this model, parasite burden (Figure 3B) and the dynamics of red cell loss (Figure 3C) are both matched between first and second infection – this eliminates pathogen load as a confounding factor when analysing acquired mechanisms of disease tolerance.
evidence: Supported by red cell count data shown in Figure 3C comparing first and second infections.

claim: The bone marrow does not prioritise the production of myeloid cells upon reinfection with malaria.
source: In contrast to a first malaria episode, the bone marrow does not prioritise the production of myeloid cells upon reinfection (Figure 3D) and preserves its cellularity and structural integrity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D and histology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The bone marrow preserves its cellularity and structural integrity upon reinfection with malaria.
source: In contrast to a first malaria episode, the bone marrow does not prioritise the production of myeloid cells upon reinfection (Figure 3D) and preserves its cellularity and structural integrity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by histology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The number of inflammatory monocytes and neutrophils released into circulation does not increase upon reinfection with malaria.
source: Consequently, the number of inflammatory monocytes and neutrophils released into circulation does not increase and nor does their accumulation in the spleen (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The spleen maintains its boundaries between red and white pulp upon reinfection with malaria.
source: Furthermore, the spleen maintains its boundaries between red and white pulp and does not promote extramedullary erythropoiesis (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by histology data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The spleen does not promote extramedullary erythropoiesis upon reinfection with malaria.
source: Furthermore, the spleen maintains its boundaries between red and white pulp and does not promote extramedullary erythropoiesis (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3D and histology in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages are resistant to malaria-induced ablation upon reinfection.
source: And whilst first infection obliterates tissue-resident macrophages these cells are resistant to malaria-induced ablation second time around (Figure 3F); this allows the host to retain ferric iron stores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3F and histology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A single malaria episode is sufficient to disarm emergency myelopoiesis in the bone marrow.
source: A single malaria episode is therefore sufficient to disarm emergency myelopoiesis in the bone marrow and protect terminally differentiated macrophages in the spleen.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations that upon reinfection, emergency myelopoiesis does not occur and macrophages are protected.

claim: A single malaria episode is sufficient to protect terminally differentiated macrophages in the spleen.
source: A single malaria episode is therefore sufficient to disarm emergency myelopoiesis in the bone marrow and protect terminally differentiated macrophages in the spleen.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that tissue-resident macrophages are not ablated during reinfection.

claim: Tissue architecture is preserved during reinfection with malaria.
source: What's more, tissue architecture is preserved and key homeostatic processes are maintained in tolerised hosts.
evidence: This is an inference based on histological observations showing maintained tissue structure during reinfection.

claim: Key homeostatic processes are maintained in tolerised hosts during reinfection with malaria.
source: What's more, tissue architecture is preserved and key homeostatic processes are maintained in tolerised hosts.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations such as maintained iron stores and normal myelopoiesis during reinfection.

claim: More than 3000 differentially expressed genes were identified in spleen monocytes during the acute phase of second infection.
source: We identified more than 3000 differentially expressed genes and found that most of these were unique to reinfection (Figure 4A); remarkably, monocytes did not differentiate into inflammatory macrophages and all functions associated with this fate were silenced (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Most differentially expressed genes in spleen monocytes during second infection were unique to reinfection.
source: We identified more than 3000 differentially expressed genes and found that most of these were unique to reinfection (Figure 4A); remarkably, monocytes did not differentiate into inflammatory macrophages and all functions associated with this fate were silenced (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A comparing first and second infections.

claim: Monocytes did not differentiate into inflammatory macrophages during second infection.
source: We identified more than 3000 differentially expressed genes and found that most of these were unique to reinfection (Figure 4A); remarkably, monocytes did not differentiate into inflammatory macrophages and all functions associated with this fate were silenced (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4B-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Circulating levels of CXCL10 and IFNɣ were attenuated at the peak of second infection.
source: Host control of inflammation extended beyond the boundaries of the spleen with circulating levels of CXCL10 and IFNɣ also attenuated at the peak of second infection (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4D measuring plasma cytokine levels.

claim: Spleen monocytes were not polarised towards alternatively activated macrophages during second infection.
source: We therefore explored alternative monocyte fates, such as those associated with immune regulation, wound healing, and tissue repair. However, spleen monocytes were not polarised towards alternatively activated macrophages and nor did they induce signature genes associated with myeloid-derived suppressor cells (Gabrilovich, 2017) or reparative Ly6Clo monocytes (Jung et al., 2017; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4E and citations to Gabrilovich, 2017 and Jung et al., 2017.

claim: Spleen monocytes did not induce signature genes associated with myeloid-derived suppressor cells during second infection.
source: We therefore explored alternative monocyte fates, such as those associated with immune regulation, wound healing, and tissue repair. However, spleen monocytes were not polarised towards alternatively activated macrophages and nor did they induce signature genes associated with myeloid-derived suppressor cells (Gabrilovich, 2017) or reparative Ly6Clo monocytes (Jung et al., 2017; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4E and citation to Gabrilovich, 2017.

claim: Spleen monocytes did not upregulate anti-inflammatory cytokines or checkpoint inhibitors during second infection.
source: Furthermore, they did not upregulate anti-inflammatory cytokines or checkpoint inhibitors (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All major supergroups in second infection related to regulation of cell cycle and nuclear division.
source: In contrast to first infection, we found minimal enrichment of GO terms linked to host defence; instead, all major supergroups in second infection related to regulation of cell cycle and nuclear division (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by clueGO analysis data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Localised proliferation of monocytes may support a critical spleen response without having to engage increased production and recruitment from the bone marrow.
source: This localised proliferation of monocytes may support a critical spleen response without having to engage increased production and recruitment from the bone marrow.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that monocytes upregulate cell cycle genes during second infection.

claim: Spleen monocytes upregulate S100a8 and S100a9 during second infection.
source: First off, they upregulate the expression of two alarmins (S100a8 and S100a9) (Figure 5D) that form the heterodimer calprotectin; this acts as an endogenous TLR4 ligand to silence the inflammatory response to pathogen-derived or damage-associated signals.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: S100a8 and S100a9 form the heterodimer calprotectin which acts as an endogenous TLR4 ligand to silence the inflammatory response.
source: First off, they upregulate the expression of two alarmins (S100a8 and S100a9) (Figure 5D) that form the heterodimer calprotectin; this acts as an endogenous TLR4 ligand to silence the inflammatory response to pathogen-derived or damage-associated signals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the function of calprotectin.

claim: Increased expression of S100a8 and S100a9 in early life prevents hyperinflammation to protect neonates from sepsis.
source: Notably, increased expression of these alarmins in early life prevents hyperinflammation to protect neonates from sepsis (Ulas et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ulas et al., 2017 which demonstrated this protective role in neonates.

claim: Chi3l1 is upregulated in monocytes during second infection and can attenuate inflammasome activation to minimise collateral tissue damage.
source: Similarly, Chi3l1 (encoding the prototypical chitinase-like protein) is also upregulated in second infection and can attenuate inflammasome activation to minimise collateral tissue damage (Dela Cruz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (implied from context) and citation to Dela Cruz et al., 2012.

claim: Monocytes upregulate Sod2 in first infection, which encodes a mitochondrial protein required to safeguard inflammatory macrophages from reactive oxygen species.
source: For example, in first infection monocytes upregulate Sod2, which encodes a mitochondrial protein required to safeguard inflammatory macrophages from the reactive oxygen species that they produce.
evidence: This combines gene expression data (implied from context) with established knowledge about Sod2 function.

claim: Monocytes upregulate Sod3 in second infection, which can be secreted to inactivate extracellular reactive oxygen species in the surrounding tissue.
source: But in second infection they instead upregulate Sod3, which can be secreted to inactivate extracellular reactive oxygen species in the surrounding tissue (Yao et al., 2010; Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 5D and citation to Yao et al., 2010.

claim: Monocytes upregulate Ednra during second infection, which can scavenge endothelin-1 to prevent vasoconstriction and hypertension.
source: In much the same way, monocytes minimise host stress by upregulating Ednra, which can scavenge endothelin-1 to prevent vasoconstriction and hypertension (Czopek et al., 2019), and they increase expression of Vegfa to promote angiogenesis.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (implied from context) and citation to Czopek et al., 2019.

claim: Monocytes increase expression of Vegfa during second infection to promote angiogenesis.
source: In much the same way, monocytes minimise host stress by upregulating Ednra, which can scavenge endothelin-1 to prevent vasoconstriction and hypertension (Czopek et al., 2019), and they increase expression of Vegfa to promote angiogenesis.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (implied from context) and established knowledge about Vegfa function.

claim: Monocytes differentially regulate heme-iron metabolism during second infection to deal with the release of toxic free heme and reactive iron from ruptured red cells.
source: In support of this argument, monocytes differentially regulate heme-iron metabolism to deal with the release of toxic free heme and reactive iron (Fe2+) from ruptured red cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Monocytes increase transcription of genes required to sequester extracellular iron, import sequestered iron for detoxification, and export detoxified iron during second infection.
source: In brief, they increase their transcription of a core set of genes required to sequester extracellular iron (Ltf encoding lactotransferrin), import sequestered iron for detoxification (Tfr1/Tfr2 encoding the transferrin receptors) and then export detoxified iron for use in the production of new red cells (Slc40a1 encoding ferroportin).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (shown in Figure 5E) and established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claim: Monocytes do not appear to increase their iron storage capacity during second infection.
source: Notably, monocytes do not appear to increase their iron storage capacity, which has been associated with tissue damage in malaria (Gozzelino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from gene expression data and citation to Gozzelino et al., 2012 regarding iron storage and tissue damage.

claim: Monocytes do not upregulate expression of heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1) during second infection.
source: And nor do they upregulate expression of heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox1), which is required to detoxify free heme.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (shown in Figure 5E).

claim: Monocytes specifically enhance iron recycling to promote tolerance to hemolysis during reinfection.
source: These data therefore indicate that monocytes specifically enhance iron recycling to promote tolerance to hemolysis – a major source of stress in malaria. Crucially, this only occurs during reinfection, despite an identical red cell loss in naive and tolerised hosts (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential regulation of iron metabolism genes during second infection compared to first infection, despite matched red cell loss.

claim: Spleen monocytes initiate a transcriptional programme designed to promote tolerance to malaria parasites upon reinfection.
source: Taken together, these data clearly show that spleen monocytes initiate a transcriptional programme designed to promote tolerance to malaria parasites upon reinfection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective observations about monocyte gene expression during second infection.

claim: Tolerance to malaria is achieved by minimising inflammation to reduce collateral tissue damage and by engaging pathways that can impart stress tolerance on the environment.
source: This is achieved in two ways – first by minimising inflammation to reduce collateral tissue damage and second by engaging pathways that can impart stress tolerance on their environment.
evidence: This is an inference summarizing the mechanisms of tolerance observed in the study.

claim: Parasite-derived signals may be sufficient to redirect monocyte fate during reinfection.
source: Significantly, mice were first infected with the avirulent parasite genotype AS, suggesting that parasite-derived signals may be sufficient to redirect monocyte fate.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that first infection with AS (avirulent) is sufficient to induce tolerance mechanisms during reinfection with AJ (virulent).

claim: Monocytes switched from upregulating the glucose transporter Slc2a1 in first infection to Slc2a3 in second infection.
source: We found that both pathways were comparably induced during first and second infection with one notable exception: monocytes switched from upregulating the glucose transporter Slc2a1 in first infection to Slc2a3 in second infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Slc2a3 encodes the facilitative GLUT3 transporter, which can continue to import glucose under hypoglycaemic conditions.
source: Slc2a3 encodes the facilitative GLUT3 transporter, which unlike most other transporters can continue to import glucose under hypoglycaemic conditions (Simpson et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simpson et al., 2008 which characterized GLUT3 function.

claim: Switching to GLUT3 may constitute a cell-intrinsic adaptation that allows monocytes to tolerate infection-induced stress.
source: Switching to GLUT3 may therefore constitute a cell-intrinsic adaptation that allows monocytes to tolerate infection-induced stress.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known function of GLUT3 and its upregulation during second infection.

claim: Monocytes differentially expressed their mitochondrial carrier proteins during first and second infection.
source: When we looked deeper into the transcriptional control of cell metabolism we found that monocytes also differentially expressed their mitochondrial carrier proteins (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Mitochondrial carrier proteins facilitate the complex crosstalk between all major metabolic pathways.
source: These membrane-embedded proteins provide the cellular wiring that connects metabolic reactions in the cytosol with the mitochondrial matrix by transporting metabolites, nucleotides, and co-enzymes across the inner mitochondrial membrane (Palmieri, 2013); in this way, mitochondrial carrier proteins facilitate the complex crosstalk between all major metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Palmieri, 2013.

claim: Spleen monocytes primarily upregulate Slc25a1 during first infection, whose major substrate is citrate.
source: In first infection, spleen monocytes primarily upregulate a carrier protein (encoded by Slc25a1) whose major substrate is citrate, a metabolite known to accumulate in inflammatory macrophages.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (shown in Figure 5F) and established knowledge about citrate accumulation in inflammatory macrophages.

claim: Monocytes upregulate Slc25a29 during reinfection, which shuttles arginine that can be fluxed through the arginase pathway to promote tolerance and wound healing.
source: In contrast, monocytes upregulate Slc25a29 during reinfection and this carrier protein shuttles arginine, which can be fluxed through the arginase pathway to promote tolerance and wound healing (O'Neill et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (shown in Figure 5F) and citation to O'Neill et al., 2016.

claim: By re-wiring their mitochondria, monocytes may be enabling their specialised tissue protective functions in tolerised hosts.
source: By re-wiring their mitochondria, monocytes may thus be enabling their specialised tissue protective functions in tolerised hosts.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential expression of mitochondrial carrier proteins during second infection.

claim: Angiopoietin-2 is the best biomarker of endothelium activation and dysfunction in human malaria and the most accurate prognostic marker of mortality in children.
source: To directly show that this coincides with a reduction in pathology we measured circulating levels of Angiopoietin-2. This vascular growth factor is the best biomarker of endothelium activation and dysfunction in human malaria and the most accurate prognostic marker of mortality in children (Yeo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yeo et al., 2008 which established Angiopoietin-2 as a biomarker in malaria.

claim: Angiopoietin-2 levels increased by more than an order of magnitude during first infection but did not deviate from a healthy uninfected baseline during second infection.
source: We found that in first infection Angiopoietin-2 levels increased by more than an order of magnitude but in second infection – with an identical parasite burden – levels did not deviate from a healthy uninfected baseline (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5G measuring Angiopoietin-2 levels.

claim: A single malaria episode can induce host adaptations that promote disease tolerance and provide long-lived clinical immunity.
source: A single malaria episode can therefore induce host adaptations that promote disease tolerance and provide long-lived clinical immunity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Angiopoietin-2 levels remain normal during second infection despite identical parasite burden.

claim: In almost every case the histone modification profiles of tolerised and specialised genes were identical between monocytes isolated from once-infected mice and uninfected controls.
source: Remarkably however, we found that in almost every case the histone modification profiles of tolerised and specialised genes were identical between monocytes isolated from once-infected mice and uninfected controls (Figure 6A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 6A-B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 95% of the 2848 tolerised/specialised genes had no detectable histone modifications in bone marrow monocytes from once-infected mice.
source: Even when we used HOMER to call differentially modified regions (DMR) and quantify differences between once-infected and control mice, we found little evidence to support epigenetic reprogramming of monocytes – of the 2848 tolerised/specialised genes identified by RNAseq 95% had no detectable histone modifications (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Innate memory can not easily explain the widespread transcriptional changes that lead to the functional specialisation of monocytes in tolerised hosts.
source: Innate memory can not therefore easily explain the widespread transcriptional changes that lead to the functional specialisation of monocytes in tolerised hosts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of epigenetic reprogramming observed in bone marrow monocytes.

claim: 111 differentially expressed genes were found in monocytes isolated from once-infected mice compared to uninfected controls.
source: We found 111 differentially expressed genes in monocytes isolated from once-infected mice compared to uninfected controls; remarkably, most of these genes were not differentially expressed during acute or chronic infection.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing once-infected mice to uninfected controls.

claim: Most of the 111 differentially expressed genes in monocytes from once-infected mice were not differentially expressed during acute or chronic infection.
source: We found 111 differentially expressed genes in monocytes isolated from once-infected mice compared to uninfected controls; remarkably, most of these genes were not differentially expressed during acute or chronic infection.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing different infection stages.

claim: The transcriptional signature unique to the memory phase was further enhanced upon reinfection.
source: Instead, this transcriptional signature was unique to the memory phase and was further enhanced upon reinfection (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 7A comparing memory and second infection.

claim: The transcription factor Maf, which regulates macrophage programming in vivo, is part of the unique transcriptional signature in memory monocytes.
source: This included the transcription factor Maf, which regulates macrophage programming in vivo (Kang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020), and Sirpa, which regulates recognition of self (Bian et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (shown in Figure 7A) and citations to Kang et al., 2017 and Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Sirpa, which regulates recognition of self, is part of the unique transcriptional signature in memory monocytes.
source: This included the transcription factor Maf, which regulates macrophage programming in vivo (Kang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2020), and Sirpa, which regulates recognition of self (Bian et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data (shown in Figure 7A) and citation to Bian et al., 2016.

claim: The majority of genes in the memory transcriptional signature related to cell cycle and nuclear division.
source: The majority of genes, however, related to cell cycle and nuclear division – specialised functions of spleen monocytes in tolerised hosts.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data and GO analysis (shown in Figure 7A-B).

claim: There is remarkable overlap in the top GO terms identified in memory and second infection.
source: Indeed, we found remarkable overlap in the top GO terms identified in memory and second infection (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A critical part of the transcriptional programme designed to promote tolerance to malaria parasites is already engaged in monocytes prior to reinfection.
source: A critical part of the transcriptional programme designed to promote tolerance to malaria parasites is therefore already engaged in monocytes prior to reinfection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that memory monocytes have a unique transcriptional signature that overlaps with second infection.

claim: The transcriptional signature in memory monocytes does not appear to require epigenetic reprogramming in the bone marrow.
source: And this transcriptional signature does not appear to require epigenetic reprogramming in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of epigenetic changes observed in bone marrow monocytes from once-infected mice.

claim: Malaria may remodel the spleen to imprint tolerance.
source: These data thus provide compelling evidence that malaria may remodel the spleen to imprint tolerance.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that monocytes are transcriptionally reprogrammed in the spleen but not epigenetically reprogrammed in the bone marrow.

claim: Mechanisms of disease tolerance can persist after pathogen clearance to minimise tissue damage, stress and pathology during subsequent infections.
source: In this study, we show that mechanisms of disease tolerance can persist after pathogen clearance to minimise tissue damage, stress and pathology during subsequent infections.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from all the experimental observations in the study.

claim: Inducible mechanisms of tolerance provide memory and constitute an alternative strategy of acquired immunity.
source: These inducible mechanisms of tolerance therefore provide memory and constitute an alternative strategy of acquired immunity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that tolerance mechanisms persist after pathogen clearance and are recalled during reinfection.

claim: Emergency myelopoiesis is disarmed during reinfection with malaria.
source: Crucially, all of these adaptations operate independently of pathogen load and limit the damage caused by malaria parasites in subsequent infections. Acquired immunity to malaria therefore prioritises host fitness over pathogen clearance.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing no increase in myeloid progenitors during second infection.

claim: Acquired mechanisms of disease tolerance operate independently of pathogen load.
source: These adaptations operate independently of pathogen load and coincide with a reduction in systemic inflammation; what's more, tissue integrity is preserved, ferric iron stores are maintained and endothelium activation/dysfunction is avoided during reinfection.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design showing matched parasite burden between first and second infection, yet different outcomes.

claim: Acquired mechanisms of disease tolerance can avert hallmark features of severe malaria.
source: Acquired mechanisms of disease tolerance can therefore avert hallmark features of severe malaria.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations such as reduced Angiopoietin-2 levels, maintained tissue architecture, and preserved iron stores during reinfection.

claim: Tissue printing of immune cell function allows monocytes to take on a remarkably diverse range of organ-specific roles.
source: Tissue printing of immune cell function is well recognised, and allows monocytes to take on a remarkably diverse range of organ-specific roles. This has been best characterised during the differentiation of monocytes into long-lived tissue resident macrophages, in which local signals imprint specialised functions that are unique to every tissue (Scott et al., 2016; van de Laar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Scott et al., 2016 and van de Laar et al., 2016.

claim: Red pulp macrophages isolated from once-infected mice are transcriptionally identical to those from uninfected controls.
source: We find that red pulp macrophages isolated from once-infected mice are transcriptionally identical to those from uninfected controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which shows that tissue printing can precisely match the transcriptional programme of recruited monocytes with the functional requirements of the tissue – in this case, to re-establish ferric iron stores.
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Malaria pigment can suppress the oxidative burst in human monocytes in vitro.
source: In support of this idea, malaria pigment can suppress the oxidative burst (Schwarzer et al., 1992) and interferon-induced upregulation of class II MHC (Schwarzer et al., 1998) in human monocytes in vitro.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwarzer et al., 1992 and Schwarzer et al., 1998.

claim: Malaria pigment can suppress interferon-induced upregulation of class II MHC in human monocytes in vitro.
source: In support of this idea, malaria pigment can suppress the oxidative burst (Schwarzer et al., 1992) and interferon-induced upregulation of class II MHC (Schwarzer et al., 1998) in human monocytes in vitro.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwarzer et al., 1998.

claim: Tissue remodelling and the accumulation of malaria pigment is observed in the human spleen.
source: Importantly, tissue remodelling and the accumulation of malaria pigment is observed in the human spleen (Buffet et al., 2011), and we therefore suggest that this is a conserved strategy through which malaria imprints tolerance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buffet et al., 2011 which documented these features in human spleens.

claim: Peak AJ parasitaemia is reduced from 25% in naive hosts to 0.5% in tolerised hosts in the reinfection model.
source: Other changes to the niche include the appearance of malaria-specific memory B and T cells, which provide effective adaptive immunity in our reinfection model (peak AJ parasitaemia is reduced from 25% in naive hosts to 0.5% in tolerised hosts).
evidence: This is data from the reinfection experiments comparing first and second infections.

claim: Phagocytosis of immune complexes in the context of Toll-like receptor signaling can induce M2 macrophages.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that phagocytosis of immune complexes in the context of Toll-like receptor signaling can induce M2 (or regulatory) macrophages (Guilliams et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guilliams et al., 2014.

claim: Malaria-specific opsonising antibodies have been directly shown to promote inflammation in human macrophages.
source: However, in these experiments M2 macrophages increased production of the pyrogenic cytokines IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF, and malaria-specific opsonising antibodies have been directly shown to promote inflammation in human macrophages (Osier et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Osier et al., 2014 and Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: Malaria-specific memory T cells have been shown to adopt new effector functions upon recall.
source: In this context, it is notable that malaria-specific memory T cells have been shown to adopt new effector functions upon recall (Zander et al., 2017); as such, they may be well placed to modify the availability of diverse signals within the tissue niche.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zander et al., 2017.

claim: Systemic inflammation can push haematopoietic stem cells down the myeloid path.
source: Current evidence indicates that systemic inflammation, which can push haematopoietic stem cells (HSC) down the myeloid path (Mitroulis et al., 2018), is triggered in the bone marrow by plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC), which produce type I interferon (Spaulding et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitroulis et al., 2018 and Spaulding et al., 2016.

claim: Systemic inflammation is triggered in the bone marrow by plasmacytoid dendritic cells, which produce type I interferon.
source: Current evidence indicates that systemic inflammation, which can push haematopoietic stem cells (HSC) down the myeloid path (Mitroulis et al., 2018), is triggered in the bone marrow by plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC), which produce type I interferon (Spaulding et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spaulding et al., 2016.

claim: Free heme is toxic to tissue-resident macrophages.
source: We suggest that the release and catabolism of free heme from ruptured red cells can explain this phenomenon. Free heme is toxic to tissue-resident macrophages (Cambos and Scorza, 2011; Ferreira et al., 2008; Haldar et al., 2014; Theurl et al., 2016) and the detoxification of free heme is known to confer disease tolerance (Seixas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cambos and Scorza, 2011; Ferreira et al., 2008; Haldar et al., 2014; Theurl et al., 2016.

claim: The detoxification of free heme is known to confer disease tolerance.
source: Free heme is toxic to tissue-resident macrophages (Cambos and Scorza, 2011; Ferreira et al., 2008; Haldar et al., 2014; Theurl et al., 2016) and the detoxification of free heme is known to confer disease tolerance (Seixas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seixas et al., 2009.

claim: Acquired immunity to malaria is often considered to be slow and ineffective, but this is only true if we consider resistance in isolation.
source: Acquired immunity to malaria is often considered to be slow and ineffective – but this is only true if we consider resistance (the ability to eliminate parasites) in isolation.
evidence: This is an inference that challenges the conventional view by distinguishing between resistance and tolerance.

claim: Mechanisms of disease tolerance provide an alternative strategy of acquired immunity that functions not to kill parasites but to limit the damage that they can cause.
source: We therefore argue that mechanisms of disease tolerance provide an alternative strategy of acquired immunity that functions not to kill parasites but to limit the damage that they can cause.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from all the experimental observations in the study.
